approachQuestion.prompt:
Calibration stripe. Given a read-only rectangular numeric matrix with R rows and C columns, return the sum of entries whose row index equals their column index. There are 1 <= R,C <= 2,000. Every entry and the final sum fit signed 64-bit. Both dimensions and any matrix entry are available in constant time through indexed access; the matrix is already in memory and its construction is outside this task. Choose minimum worst-case time, then auxiliary space. Return one integer.

Example 1: Input: matrix=[[3,8,2],[6,-1,9]]. Output: 2 (3 plus -1).
Example 2: Input: matrix=[[4],[7],[2]]. Output: 4.

options.text: For i from zero up to but excluding the smaller dimension, add matrix[i][i] to a running total.
options.feedback: Exactly these positions satisfy the index condition, and direct access avoids inspecting unrelated cells.

options.text: Visit every matrix cell, adding its value only when the row and column indices match.
options.feedback: It gives the correct sum but inspects all off-stripe cells. For a large square matrix, direct indexing skips nearly all of that unnecessary work.

options.text: Read matrix[i][i] for every i below the larger dimension.
options.feedback: For a 3-by-1 matrix, i=1 tries to access a nonexistent column. The stripe ends when either dimension ends.

options.text: Return the sum of the first row.
options.feedback: For matrix=[[3,8],[6,-1]], this gives 11 instead of the stripe sum 2.

feedback.reason: Already available random access can avoid reading input positions that cannot affect the answer.
details: Set the total to zero. Let d be the smaller of R and C. For each i from 0 through d-1, add matrix[i][i] and return the total. No matrix copy is made.

In a 2-by-5 matrix, only (0,0) and (1,1) satisfy equal row and column indices. The diagonal ends when either dimension ends. Random access lets the method visit these cells directly; a forward-only representation would not justify skipping every other entry at no cost.

“For i from zero up to but excluding the smaller dimension, add matrix[i][i] to a running total.”: Exactly these positions satisfy the index condition, and direct access avoids inspecting unrelated cells.

“Visit every matrix cell, adding its value only when the row and column indices match.”: It gives the correct sum but inspects all off-stripe cells. For a large square matrix, direct indexing skips nearly all of that unnecessary work.
“Read matrix[i][i] for every i below the larger dimension.”: For a 3-by-1 matrix, i=1 tries to access a nonexistent column. The stripe ends when either dimension ends.
“Return the sum of the first row.”: For matrix=[[3,8],[6,-1]], this gives 11 instead of the stripe sum 2.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For index-the-stripe, what are worst-case time and auxiliary space? Count only this computation on the already provided matrix, not construction or transport of the input. R and C are independent positive dimensions.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

feedback.reason: Read min(R,C) diagonal cells with fixed helper state.
details: There are exactly min(R,C) valid equal-index positions, each directly read once. A total, index, and bound require constant storage. Reading the entire matrix is not required by the random-access input model. No hashing, recursion, or copying is involved.
“O(RC) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: That is the cost of examining every cell, not the tight bound for the indexed stripe traversal.
“O(max(R,C)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The shorter dimension ends the stripe; with C=1, only one cell is read even if R grows.
“O(min(R,C)) time, O(min(R,C)) auxiliary space”: The values are added as read; no separate stripe array is created.
